This is a range. Should I create model_level entries? The rule says lists of values → model matrix. But this is a continuous range "60 kg up to and including 5000 kg". I think it's best as a type_level characteristic with value {min: 60, max: 5000}, unit kg. Since it's a range not discrete variants, no model_family needed. But rule 4 says detect family of models where attributes vary per model. Here there's just one range. I'll keep type_level with min/max.

The schema value shape only allows number | {min,max} | string. I could use {min: 350, max: 450} with unit "Ω". But that loses the nominal. Alternatively value: "400 ± 50", unit_symbol: "Ω". I think {min: 350, max: 450} is cleaner and consistent with the structured-value rules. Hmm, but tolerance vs range... The rule says ranges become {min, max}. A ± tolerance is effectively a range. I'll do {min: 350, max: 450}, unit Ω. Actually, maybe better to keep nominal separate. I'll add "input_impedance_nominal": 400 and "input_impedance_tolerance": 50? That might be over-engineering. I'll go with {min: 350, max: 450} for input_impedance and {min: 350, max: 354} for output_impedance (352 ± 2). Hmm, 352±2 = 350 to 354.

Alternatively, keep it as string "400 ± 50" with unit Ω. The rules say numbers not strings, but tolerance isn't strictly a range... I'll use min/max since it's most machine-readable.

Here "10 V AC / DC" → recommended_excitation: 10 V, and excitation_type: "AC / DC". I'll do recommended_excitation: {value: 10, unit_symbol: "V"} and maybe "recommended_excitation_type": "AC / DC". Similarly excitation_maximum: 15 V, type AC/DC. I could add a shared "excitation_type": "AC / DC" but it applies to both. I'll include excitation_type once as type_level: "AC / DC". Hmm, or attach to each. Simpler: recommended_excitation_voltage 10 V, maximum_excitation_voltage 15 V, excitation_type "AC / DC". Keep labels close to source: "recommended_excitation", "excitation_maximum", "excitation_type".

- atmospheric_protection: "Hermetically sealed"

I'll add "us_accuracy_class" as type_level characteristic? Hmm, might be noise. I'll add it since it's a real certified characteristic: "us_accuracy_class": "III L". Actually the Utilizer Declaration compliance is a statement; including it seems reasonable but optional. I'll include "us_accuracy_class_nist_hb44": "III L"? Keep it simple: skip, or include "additional_us_accuracy_class": "III L". I'll include accuracy_classes: ["C"] in recommendation and add a type_level "us_accuracy_class": "III L". Hmm. Risk of fabrication? No, it's in the doc. I'll include it.

Actually schema says module_designation # "Analog load cell" | "Not applicable" | null. I'll go with "Analog load cell" as canonical per schema... Hmm. I'll use "Analog load cell" per schema canon, since that's the canonical label the schema wants. Actually being faithful is safer: "Analog-passive load cell". The schema comment is just examples. I'll use "Analog load cell" — no wait. Rule 8: don't fabricate. "Analog-passive load cell" is what's there. Use that.

description: "A tension load cell, with strain gauges. Registered trade name: Minebea Intec."

manufacturers: same as applicant: Minebea Intec GmbH.

For kg, the example schema shows "u:degree_Celsius" pattern; kg might be "u:kilogram" but I'm not 100% certain — leave null. I'll only set degree_Celsius which was explicitly exemplified.
